screens.title: FBX vs glTF — choose the right format
screens.narratorSegment: FBX and glTF are the two formats you’ll use most for game asset exchange. Start by defining each format: FBX is a long-established, feature-rich format frequently used when you need complex scene data, legacy pipeline compatibility, or animation and rig support. glTF is an open, compact format optimized for fast loading and modern PBR materials; the binary. glb bundles everything into a single file. A concrete example: if you are exporting a skinned, animated character with a complex rig and animation clips for a production game, FBX often provides the most reliable transfer. If you are exporting a static prop with PBR textures for a web viewer or a real-time UI where load size matters,. glb is an excellent choice. A common misconception is that glTF cannot handle animations—it can, but FBX historically has broader support across older pipelines and tools. Key takeaway: pick glTF for streamlined PBR workflows and web use, pick FBX for maximum compatibility and complex scene data. Always confirm the target engine’s preferred format and test the import before committing to a pipeline. FBX vs glTF — choose the right format means use fbx for legacy pipelines and complex rigged data; use gltf/.glb for compact pbr assets and fast loading in modern engines or web viewers.. In practical terms, strengths, trade-offs, and when to prefer each for game exports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › FBX vs glTF
Core Concept

FBX and glTF compared

Understand each format's role so you choose the one that minimizes post-import fixes.

  • FBX: stores animations, rigging, multiple channels and is widely supported across engines. Example: exporting a skinned character with baked animations.
  • glTF/.glb: compact, PBR-friendly, often embeds textures and meshes in one file, ideal for web or fast runtime loads.
  • Misconception check: glTF can include animations but verify your engine’s importer features before relying on full animation transfer.
Key Takeaway

Select the format that matches your engine needs: compatibility versus compactness. Test imports early.

FBX — When to use
Complex animations, legacy pipelines, and when your engine expects FBX for rigging fidelity.
Example: exporting a character with multiple animation clips and skin weights.
glTF/.glb — When to use
Static props and PBR materials for web or fast runtime loading where file size matters.
Example: a prop with embedded base color and roughness maps in a single .glb file.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm engine format preference
  • Decide on single-file vs. separate textures
  • Plan for animations or static export only

screens.title: FBX Export Settings in Blender
screens.narratorSegment: Exporting FBX from Blender requires attention to several sections of the export dialogue. Start by selecting the objects you actually want to export and enable Selected Objects to avoid accidental scene geometry. Under Object Types, ensure Mesh is checked for static props. In the Transform group set Apply Scalings to a consistent option—'FBX All' or 'FBX Units Scale'—so Blender's units translate correctly. Coordinate axes are critical: Unity commonly expects Forward = -Z and Up = Y, while Unreal prefers Z-up. If your model imports sideways, that's the axis mismatch. For geometry, enable Apply Modifiers if you want modifier results baked into the exported mesh; otherwise, the engine will see the base mesh only. For textures, set Path Mode to Copy and check Embed Textures if you want a single file containing images. A common mistake is forgetting to embed textures or pack them into the. blend, which leaves the engine unable to find the images. After export, always test import into your target engine and adjust settings as necessary. FBX Export Settings in Blender means selected objects, mesh object type, apply scalings, forward/up axes for engine, apply modifiers, and embed textures when desired.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › FBX Export Settings
Process Flow

FBX Export Steps

  1. Select your mesh objects and enable Selected Objects in export.
  2. Set Object Types → Mesh to ensure only geometry exports.
  3. Transform → Apply Scalings: use FBX All or Units Scale for consistent size.
  4. Set Forward/Up to match the target engine (example: -Z / Y for Unity).
  5. Geometry → Apply Modifiers if you need modifier results baked into the mesh.
  6. Path Mode → Copy and Embed Textures to include images in the FBX.
Key Takeaway

FBX export has many toggles; use Selected Objects and match axes and scale for predictable imports.

Transform settings
Apply Scalings and Forward/Up axes control orientation and size. Mismatches cause sideways or flipped imports.
Geometry
Apply Modifiers to bake changes. If left unapplied, the engine receives the pre-modifier mesh.
Textures
Use Path Mode Copy and Embed to include textures in the FBX. Otherwise pack your .blend first.
Common mistake
Forgetting Selected Objects exports the entire scene, including cameras and lights.

screens.title: glTF Export Essentials (.glb vs .gltf)
screens.narratorSegment: glTF is designed for efficient transmission and real-time rendering. The two container options are. gltf, which is JSON plus external binary and image files, and. glb, which packs binary geometry and images into a single binary file. Use. glb when you want a single distributable file that includes textures and meshes—this is convenient for web viewers and simple imports. If your pipeline prefers separate image assets, export. gltf and keep textures external. To preserve PBR materials, make sure PBR Materials or Principled BSDF translation is enabled so Base Color, Roughness, Metallic, and Normal maps carry across. A practical example: export a textured crate as. glb to avoid broken paths in a web viewer. A common misconception is that glTF cannot represent PBR properly. It can, and it often preserves Principled shader properties well, but always inspect the exported material maps in the engine or viewer. Definition

glTF formats and PBR materials

Know whether to export .glb or .gltf and how to preserve Principled materials for real-time use.

.glb
Single-file binary containing meshes and textures. Best for portability and web viewers.
.gltf
JSON file with separate binary and image files. Useful if you need to post-process textures separately.
Practical checklist
  • Choose .glb for single-file delivery; .gltf if you require external images.
  • Enable PBR Materials so Principled BSDF nodes map to glTF PBR workflow.
  • Pack or ensure image paths are correct before export to avoid missing textures.
Key Takeaway

For most web and runtime cases, .glb simplifies asset management and preserves PBR textures when exported correctly.

screens.title: Coordinate Systems & Axes
screens.narratorSegment: Coordinate systems determine how a model is oriented in space, and mismatches between Blender and a target engine are one of the most common causes of wrongly rotated imports. Blender uses Z-up as its default, but Unity typically uses Y-up and treats negative Z as forward; Unreal Engine uses Z-up. When exporting, set Forward and Up in the export dialogue to remap your mesh’s axes to the engine’s expectations. For example, to prepare assets for Unity, set Forward to -Z Forward and Up to Y Up so the model stands upright in Unity. A concrete example: exporting a character without remapping axes can cause the character to lie on its back after import. A common misconception is that reorienting the object in Blender solves the axis issue; reorientation without matching export axes can still produce incorrect results because Blender’s internal axis metadata differs from the exported file. Key takeaway: match the forward and up axes in export settings to the engine’s conventions, and test with a simple import to confirm orientation. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Coordinate Systems
Process Flow

Match engine axes before export

Map Blender's axes to the engine to avoid rotated or flipped imports.

Unity example: Forward = -Z Forward, Up = Y Up.
Unreal example: Maintain Z Up if the engine expects Z-up.
Test by exporting a simple cube or your asset and importing to verify standing orientation and pivot.
Common mistake

Rotating the mesh in Blender without setting export axes often still results in wrong orientation in the engine because the export remaps axes unless configured.

Quick checks
  • Confirm Blender unit scale and export scale factor.
  • Use a test import to verify orientation before batch exporting many assets.
  • Adjust Forward/Up settings in the exporter rather than re-rotating models where possible.
Example scenario
If a model lies flat after import, revise Forward/Up mapping and re-export instead of manually re-rotating in the engine.

screens.title: Textures and Packing
screens.narratorSegment: Missing textures are a frequent and frustrating export issue. It usually happens when the engine cannot find the image files referenced by your materials. In Blender, you can pack images into the. blend file using File → External Data → Pack All Into. blend, which helps when sending the. blend to others. For FBX, set Path Mode to Copy and check Embed Textures so the exporter includes image data in the file. For glTF. glb, textures are often embedded by default in the binary file. A concrete example: you export a crate as FBX but the base color appears grey in the engine because the export left texture paths as absolute local paths; the engine cannot access them. Another common misconception is that simply leaving textures in the same folder as the exporter will always work; relative paths can break when the file moves or when the engine expects embedded images. Key takeaway: pack or embed images during export or manage relative paths carefully and test the imported result to confirm materials display correctly. In practical terms, prevent missing textures by packing or embedding and validating image paths. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Textures & Packing
Definition

Why textures go missing

Texture references break when export does not include image data or when file paths change relative to the engine.

Pack into .blend: File → External Data → Pack All Into .blend bundles images inside your Blender file.
FBX: Path Mode → Copy and check Embed Textures to include them in the FBX.
glTF/.glb: .glb typically embeds images automatically, making distribution simpler.
Practical checklist
  • Pack images into the .blend before export if you share the .blend file.
  • Prefer Embed or .glb for single-file delivery to avoid broken paths.
  • If using external images, maintain a consistent relative folder structure and test imports.
Mistake to avoid
Relying on absolute file paths on your machine will fail when the file is moved or opened elsewhere.

screens.title: Normals and Shading
screens.narratorSegment: Normals determine which side of a face is considered the outside surface and how shading interpolates across polygons. Incorrect normals lead to faceted shading, dark patches, or parts of a mesh appearing inside-out in an engine. In Blender, check Face Orientation in Viewport Overlays to reveal flipped faces in red. In Edit Mode use Select All and then Shift N to recalculate normals to point outward. For complex cases you may need to manually flip specific faces or use auto-smooth for sharp edges. A concrete example: an exported prop looks strangely shaded in the engine because several faces were inverted; recalculating normals fixes the shading without changing geometry. A common misconception is that smoothing alone will correct a shading artifact; smoothing controls interpolation but a flipped normal will still render incorrectly. Key takeaway: always inspect and correct normals as part of your export checklist; shading issues are easier to fix before export than after import. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Normals & Shading
Core Concept

Normals matter for correct shading

Flipped normals or inconsistent smoothing often cause the worst-looking shading in game engines.

  • Enable Face Orientation to spot flipped faces (red = inside).
  • In Edit Mode select all and press Shift + N to recalculate outward normals.
  • Use auto-smooth for hard edges or manually split normals where necessary.
Common misconception

Smoothing groups alone do not fix an inverted normal. The face orientation must be corrected first.

Practical example
If a part of your mesh appears dark or disappears in the engine, check normals. Recalculate and re-export to confirm the fix.
Key Takeaway

Normals fixed in Blender usually solve shading artifacts after import. Do this before export to save time.

screens.title: Apply Transforms & Modifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Transforms and modifiers control the final geometry written to export. If transforms like scale or rotation are unapplied, the exporter may write unexpected values and the model could import with the wrong size or orientation. Always use Ctrl + A and apply Location, Rotation, and Scale to bake the object’s transforms into its data. For modifiers such as Mirror or Subdivision Surface, decide whether the engine should see the results. If yes, enable Apply Modifiers in the export dialogue or apply them manually in Blender before export. If you keep them unapplied, some exporters will ignore them and the engine will receive the base mesh only. A concrete example: a mirrored model exported without applying the Mirror modifier will be missing the mirrored half in the engine. A common misconception is that exporters automatically apply modifiers; many do not by default. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting

Fix the usual export failures

  • Missing textures: pack .blend or embed images during export.
  • Scale errors: verify unit settings and export scale; try example scale values and re-import.
  • Wrong orientation: adjust Forward/Up mapping to match the engine.
  • Shading artifacts: check normals and smoothing groups.
Practical debugging flow
  1. Export a simple textured cube and import it into the engine.
  2. If cube looks correct, focus on the model-specific steps (normals, modifiers, origin).
  3. Change one exporter option at a time and re-import to find the cause.
Key Takeaway

A systematic, one-change-at-a-time approach shortens debug time and reveals which specific setting causes the problem.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on exporting static models from Blender into formats that game engines expect. You will learn the strengths of FBX and glTF, how to configure Blender's export dialogue, and how to avoid common mistakes like missing textures, flipped normals, or scale mismatches. We’ll treat FBX as the robust, feature-rich option often used for complex data and rigging, and glTF as the lean, efficient choice for real-time and web use. You’ll see concrete export settings to match Unity or Unreal’s coordinate conventions, the practical steps to pack or embed textures, and the simple transforms and modifier checks that prevent problems after import. By the end you’ll have a clear export checklist to test your asset in a target engine and iterate until it imports correctly. Think of export as translation: small mismatches break how a model looks or behaves, and knowing the right settings saves repeated edits. Keep the checklist handy and expect an iterative test-and-fix loop when you first move assets into a real project.

By the end of this chapter you will understand the two primary export formats used in game development, FBX and glTF, and be able to choose between them based on your project needs. You will learn how to navigate Blender's export dialogue and configure settings such as selected objects, transform axes, scale factors, and whether to embed textures. You will also be able to identify and fix common export problems: missing textures, incorrect normals that lead to bad shading, and scale mismatches that place models at the wrong size in the engine. Finally, you will develop a repeatable checklist to prepare a static mesh for export and perform a successful export into a target engine. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the steps when you work in Blender later. Practice these skills by exporting a prepared asset and testing it in a game scene to verify orientation, pivot, and material fidelity.

These follow-up objectives emphasize the hands-on steps that make exports reliable. You will learn to clean a scene by deleting unused objects or using the Selected Objects option to limit exports. You will practice applying transforms and modifiers so the mesh seen in Blender matches the geometry written to the file. You will also verify material compatibility, ensuring Principled BSDF-based PBR maps are present and paths are either embedded or packed. Each step reduces the number of surprises when the asset appears in the engine. The learning here is iterative: export, import, inspect, and fix. For example, you will try exporting a crate, check its pivot and scale in the engine, and then adjust the scale factor or axes in Blender and re-export. This hands-on loop is the fastest way to internalize how export settings affect final results.

FBX and glTF are the two formats you’ll use most for game asset exchange. Start by defining each format: FBX is a long-established, feature-rich format frequently used when you need complex scene data, legacy pipeline compatibility, or animation and rig support. glTF is an open, compact format optimized for fast loading and modern PBR materials; the binary. glb bundles everything into a single file. A concrete example: if you are exporting a skinned, animated character with a complex rig and animation clips for a production game, FBX often provides the most reliable transfer. If you are exporting a static prop with PBR textures for a web viewer or a real-time UI where load size matters,. glb is an excellent choice. A common misconception is that glTF cannot handle animations—it can, but FBX historically has broader support across older pipelines and tools. Key takeaway: pick glTF for streamlined PBR workflows and web use, pick FBX for maximum compatibility and complex scene data. Always confirm the target engine’s preferred format and test the import before committing to a pipeline. FBX vs glTF — choose the right format means use fbx for legacy pipelines and complex rigged data; use gltf/.glb for compact pbr assets and fast loading in modern engines or web viewers.. In practical terms, strengths, trade-offs, and when to prefer each for game exports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Exporting FBX from Blender requires attention to several sections of the export dialogue. Start by selecting the objects you actually want to export and enable Selected Objects to avoid accidental scene geometry. Under Object Types, ensure Mesh is checked for static props. In the Transform group set Apply Scalings to a consistent option—'FBX All' or 'FBX Units Scale'—so Blender's units translate correctly. Coordinate axes are critical: Unity commonly expects Forward = -Z and Up = Y, while Unreal prefers Z-up. If your model imports sideways, that's the axis mismatch. For geometry, enable Apply Modifiers if you want modifier results baked into the exported mesh; otherwise, the engine will see the base mesh only. For textures, set Path Mode to Copy and check Embed Textures if you want a single file containing images. A common mistake is forgetting to embed textures or pack them into the. blend, which leaves the engine unable to find the images. After export, always test import into your target engine and adjust settings as necessary. FBX Export Settings in Blender means selected objects, mesh object type, apply scalings, forward/up axes for engine, apply modifiers, and embed textures when desired.. In practical terms, key options to set for reliable fbx exports to unity or unreal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

glTF is designed for efficient transmission and real-time rendering. The two container options are. gltf, which is JSON plus external binary and image files, and. glb, which packs binary geometry and images into a single binary file. Use. glb when you want a single distributable file that includes textures and meshes—this is convenient for web viewers and simple imports. If your pipeline prefers separate image assets, export. gltf and keep textures external. To preserve PBR materials, make sure PBR Materials or Principled BSDF translation is enabled so Base Color, Roughness, Metallic, and Normal maps carry across. A practical example: export a textured crate as. glb to avoid broken paths in a web viewer. A common misconception is that glTF cannot represent PBR properly. It can, and it often preserves Principled shader properties well, but always inspect the exported material maps in the engine or viewer. Key takeaway: choose. glb for single-file portability and ensure PBR map export is enabled. glTF Export Essentials (.glb vs .gltf) means .glb bundles everything and is best for portability; .gltf keeps separate assets if your pipeline requires them. always enable pbr export for principled materials.. Coordinate systems determine how a model is oriented in space, and mismatches between Blender and a target engine are one of the most common causes of wrongly rotated imports. Blender uses Z-up as its default, but Unity typically uses Y-up and treats negative Z as forward; Unreal Engine uses Z-up. When exporting, set Forward and Up in the export dialogue to remap your mesh’s axes to the engine’s expectations. For example, to prepare assets for Unity, set Forward to -Z Forward and Up to Y Up so the model stands upright in Unity. A concrete example: exporting a character without remapping axes can cause the character to lie on its back after import. A common misconception is that reorienting the object in Blender solves the axis issue; reorientation without matching export axes can still produce incorrect results because Blender’s internal axis metadata differs from the exported file. Key takeaway: match the forward and up axes in export settings to the engine’s conventions, and test with a simple import to confirm orientation. Missing textures are a frequent and frustrating export issue. It usually happens when the engine cannot find the image files referenced by your materials. In Blender, you can pack images into the. blend file using File → External Data → Pack All Into. blend, which helps when sending the. blend to others. Normals determine which side of a face is considered the outside surface and how shading interpolates across polygons. Incorrect normals lead to faceted shading, dark patches, or parts of a mesh appearing inside-out in an engine. In Blender, check Face Orientation in Viewport Overlays to reveal flipped faces in red. In Edit Mode use Select All and then Shift N to recalculate normals to point outward. For complex cases you may need to manually flip specific faces or use auto-smooth for sharp edges. A concrete example: an exported prop looks strangely shaded in the engine because several faces were inverted; recalculating normals fixes the shading without changing geometry. A common misconception is that smoothing alone will correct a shading artifact; smoothing controls interpolation but a flipped normal will still render incorrectly. Transforms and modifiers control the final geometry written to export. If transforms like scale or rotation are unapplied, the exporter may write unexpected values and the model could import with the wrong size or orientation. Always use Ctrl + A and apply Location, Rotation, and Scale to bake the object’s transforms into its data. For modifiers such as Mirror or Subdivision Surface, decide whether the engine should see the results. If yes, enable Apply Modifiers in the export dialogue or apply them manually in Blender before export. If you keep them unapplied, some exporters will ignore them and the engine will receive the base mesh only. A concrete example: a mirrored model exported without applying the Mirror modifier will be missing the mirrored half in the engine. A common misconception is that exporters automatically apply modifiers; many do not by default. A compact export workflow reduces errors and saves time. Follow these steps every time you prepare a static mesh: first clean up the scene by deleting cameras, lights, and unused meshes, or ensure Selected Objects is used at export. Second, apply transforms with Ctrl + A for Location, Rotation, and Scale. Third, set the origin and pivot where you need it to be in the engine, for example the base of a prop. Fourth, recalculate normals in Edit Mode using Shift + N and verify with Face Orientation. Fifth, check materials: use Principled BSDF, confirm image node paths, and pack images or enable embed options. Sixth, apply modifiers or enable Apply Modifiers during export. Seventh, open File → Export and set format-specific options (axes, scale, embed). Third, asset fidelity depends on packing or embedding textures, correcting normals, and applying necessary modifiers so the engine sees the final geometry.
